newsitem.title: FRANCE: LEFTIST WIN ENDS SEGUIN'S HOPES FOR PREMIERSHIP.
newsitem.headline: LEFTIST WIN ENDS SEGUIN'S HOPES FOR PREMIERSHIP.

text.p: Eurosceptic Gaullist Philippe Seguin made a direct bid for the leadership of France's right on Sunday after his last-ditch bid to save the conservative coalition from election defeat floundered.

The 54-year-old outgoing National Assembly speaker, who was re-elected in his own constituency, bowed to the national vote which ended his hopes of being the next prime minister, "cruel as it can be".
But he said he was determined to prepare for a return to power "with all those who share the same conception of France, of France in Europe and to prepare for a different tomorrow".

Seguin, who led the "no" campaign in a 1992 referendum on the Maastricht Treaty on European union, was the main critic of fellow-Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe's austerity policies geared to make France meet the criteria for joining the single European currency.

He had little time to make his mark, being thrust into the limelight in an improbable "dream team" with militant free-marketeer Alain Madelin only after Juppe bowed out following last Sunday's first-round left-wing upset.

"This obsessive time...that we need to tell the French how well we understood their message," said Seguin with a hint of desperation, ending his campaign with an appeal to voters not to recall "ghosts of the past" to power.
The crisis, he said on Sunday, "is that of our whole political system, and that goes for both winners and losers of whom one does not know which to pity more".
A recent convert to a single European currency, he had promised to heed the voters' first-round warning and give precedence to the fight for jobs over budget austerity.

But analysts said the bizarre last-minute tandem could just as easily have alienated voters by further blurring President Jacques Chirac's unclear message about what policies he wants his government to follow.

His social Gaullism, with its emphasis on the role of the state in protecting the weak and jobless, has been a useful electoral counterfoil to the Juppe government's record of austerity, tax increases and record unemployment.
Seguin has also sought to distance himself from state economic "dirigisme", advocating "a tempered liberalism".
In 1992, in the campaign for the Maastricht Treaty referendum, Seguin spoke for the "no" camp in a crucial live television debate with Socialist president Francois Mitterrand who was ill with cancer.

A former law lecturer and an outstanding orator, he chose to be respectful rather than confrontational, disappointing some supporters but earning respect for his statesmanship. The treaty was passed by just 51.05 percent.
Hoping to silence him with a largely ceremonial job, the Gaullist party made Seguin National Assembly president in 1993 after the centre-right won big in general elections.
Instead, the rebel became an authoritarian and active speaker, trying to build up the Assembly's role, punishing absenteeism and reforming the parliamentary calendar.
His huge bearlike figure and deep voice became familiar to viewers as he scolded deputies like schoolchildren for rumpus in the twice-weekly televised question time.

He used his high-profile position to become the coalition's social conscience, accusing then premier Edouard Balladur of capitulating to unemployment just as the West sought to appease Hitler before World War Two.

When Chirac became president and made Juppe prime minister, Seguin continued to warn that indiscriminate budget cuts would fail to pull France out of recession and advocated a more expansionary economic policy.

Born in Tunis in 1943, Seguin never knew his father, who was killed in World War Two when he was a baby. Like many politicians, he attended the Ecole Nationale d'Administration, the forcing ground for France's ruling elite.
